newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cbank says not discussing rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Czech cbank says not discussing rate cut.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) told Reuters on Monday that it was not discussing cutting interest rates, that the current weakening of the crown was not based on fundamentals and that it was prepared to support the currency if necessary.
"Any speculation about imminent cuts in rates, which emerged on Friday, is not based on any discussion in the central bank," said Ludek Niedermeyer, CNB board member in charge of market operations.
The central bank board met last Thursday and decided to leave monetary policy unchanged but the crown continued to weaken.
On Monday morning, the crown fell to minus 3.8 percent against the mid-point of its mark/dollar fixing basket from around minus 2.3 percent at Friday's close.
"I do not think that any such relatively fast weakening as we are seeing just now is based on fundamentals. It has more of a technical nature," said Niedermeyer.

He said he thought people were overreacting in a negative way at the moment in the same way that sentiment was unduly bullish about the crown earlier this year, adding that he thought the weakening would be only short term.
"Of course we stay behind the crown, we are ready to support if necessary and we are following the market very closely," said Niedermeyer.

He said the central bank would closely monitor the effect on the liquidity of the banking sector of last week's imposition by the government of a 20 percent import deposit requirement against the value of consumer and agricultural imports.

"If we find there is a necessity to react, the nature of the import deposits is much more related to minimum reserve requirement levels, not to interest rates," he said adding that no such move was currently under consideration.

Nidermeyer said that there had been a number of new economic figures supporting the central bank's view that the crown weakening was not based on fundamentals. He said that trade figures for March were better than expected.

The Czech Republic posted a first quarter trade deficit of 40.181 billion crowns, compared to a 27.112 billion crown deficit for the same period in 1996, the Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) said last Tuesday.

The CSU said in a statement that March's trade deficit was 13.429 compared with 13.415 billion crowns in February. Analysts polled by Reuters before the announcement had been expecting a March deficit of around 17 billion crowns.
"We do have some other evidence that there is no fundamental basis for depreciation and speculation," Niedermeyer said without elaborating.
The currency markets have been rife with speculation that the CNB would soon heed government calls for a relaxation of monetary policy to boost sagging economic growth.
Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus recently halved his 1997 gross domestic product growth forecast to a maximum of 2.7 percent after 4.4 percent in 1996.
Last summer, the CNB raised the discount rate to 10.5 percent from 9.5, the Lombard rate to 14 percent from 12.5 percent and bank minimum reserve requirements to 11.5 percent from 8.5.
Two weeks ago the CNB cut reserve requirements back to 9.5 percent.
